items.title: 26.3 Identifying the Type, Repeat Unit and Monomers of a Polymer

source_refs.note: Topic 26.3 as printed (PDF 152-154): the steps, Table 26.1 and the first Quick Check 26.2 (questions only, sections written as formulas). The printed schemes are the existing figures.

blocks.text: To identify a polymer from a skeletal or structural formula, you must look for the repeating linkage and the monomer units. At this level, only two classes of polymers are under discussion
Follow the given steps to identify the type of the polymer by considering the example of poly(ethene)

items: The first thing to check is what atoms make up the main horizontal chain of the polymer, i.e to identify the backbone.
If the main chain consists only of carbon atoms (-C-C-C-C-), it is an addition polymer. These are formed from alkenes.
If the main chain contains oxygen (O) or nitrogen (N) atoms with carbon, it is a condensation polymer (like polyesters or polyamides).

blocks.text: Now, identify the functional linkage. There are again two possibilities:
i. If a carbonyl group (C=O) is directly attached next to an oxygen (O). Such polymers are classified as polyesters. For example, PET has an ester linkage in the given section of its structure.

blocks.alt: Section of PET in brackets with subscript n: -C(=O)-benzene ring-C(=O)-O-CH2-CH2-O-. A small arrow points at the C=O of the ester linkage.
blocks.caption: PET section showing its ester linkage (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 152).

blocks.text: If there is a carbonyl group (C=O) directly next to a nitrogen (N) with a hydrogen (H) attached, it presents an amide or peptide linkage. The polymer is, therefore, classified as a polyamide (e.g., Nylon 6,6 or Kevlar).

blocks.alt: Section of Kevlar: -N(H)-C(=O)-ring-C(=O)-N(H)-ring-N(H)-C(=O)-ring-C(=O)-N(H)-, with each C=O drawn upward and each N-H downward, showing the amide links between benzene rings.
blocks.caption: Kevlar section showing its amide linkages (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 152).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The table prints 'poly (tetrafluoroethen)'. The monomer is tetrafluoroethene, so the polymer is poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE.
To find the original monomers, one must first identify the smallest section that repeats itself in the section of the polymer.

items: To find the repeating pattern, look for where the sequence starts to duplicate itself. Locate such duplicating sections in the backbone.
Place brackets around one of these recurring sections and add the subscript n. This section within the brackets is the repeat unit of the polymer.

blocks.text: a) For addition polymers, change the C-C single bond in the repeat unit back into a C=C double bond to find the monomer.

blocks.alt: Part of addition polymer: a displayed chain of seven carbons with a benzene ring on every second carbon and H on the rest. An arrow leads to the repeat unit, [-CH(C6H5)-CH2-]n drawn in brackets, and another arrow to the monomer, H2C=CH(C6H5) (phenylethene).
blocks.caption: Identification of repeat unit and monomers (addition) (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 153).

blocks.text: b) For Condensation polymers: Add water back in. Break the ester or amide bond. Add -OH to the C=O side and -H to the O or N side as given below.

blocks.alt: Part of condensation polymer (Kevlar): -NH-CO-ring-CO-NH-ring-NH-CO-ring-CO-NH-. Arrow to the repeat unit [-NH-ring-NH-CO-ring-CO-]n. Arrow to the monomers: H2N-ring-NH2 and HOOC-ring-COOH, or ClOC-ring-COCl.
blocks.caption: Identification of repeat unit and monomers (condensation) (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 153, which is captioned '(addition)').

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book captions the Kevlar scheme 'Identification of repeat unit and monomers (addition)'; Kevlar is a condensation polymer (amide links), so the figure is captioned (condensation). The label printed 'monome' is completed to 'monomer'.
